tracks.title: Who does the housework?
tracks.note: Neil과 Pippa가 집안일(household chores)을 누가 얼마나 하는지 이야기해요. 인도네시아 Rote 섬의 '여자 일' 문화와, 아빠와 아들이 집안일을 배우는 크로아티아의 'Superdads' 프로젝트가 나와요. 두 아이 아빠로서 공감 가는 주제예요! 1회차는 대략적인 내용만, 2회차는 스크립트를 보면서 들어요.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Hello, this is 6 Minute English from BBC Learning English.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: I'm Neil.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: And I'm Pippa.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: When it comes to household chores, jobs like cleaning, washing clothes or looking after the kids, it's often women who do most of the work.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: Here, two female listeners of BBC World Service programme People Fixing the World share their experiences.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: Do they sound familiar to you?

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: Listener 1 I do everything.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: I do all the house chores, I do the food shopping, I do all the cooking, I clean the bathroom.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: Listener 2 Are the chores done equally between me and my husband?

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: No, they're not done equally.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: I do most of the chores.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: So, you're a family man, Neil.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: Do you do your fair share of household chores?

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: I think so.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: My wife works part time and I work full time, so when I'm not working, I do things, and when she's not working, she does things.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: Yeah, it's similar in my house, so me and my husband try to split things, but it's difficult, isn't it?

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: It is.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: Of course, no one enjoys cleaning the toilet or taking out the bins, but there is a serious side to the issue.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: Figures from UN Women, an organisation promoting gender equality, suggest that every day women around the world spend three hours more than men on unpaid care and domestic work.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: So, in this episode, we'll be hearing about two projects helping husbands and wives share the housework more fairly.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: And as usual, you'll find a quiz and a worksheet to go with this episode on our website, bbclearningenglish.com.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: But now I have a question for you, Pippa.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: According to a survey conducted by Good Housekeeping magazine earlier this year, what is the most hated household chore in Britain?

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Is it: a) deep cleaning the oven, b) scrubbing the toilet, or c) cleaning the windows?

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: Hmm.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: I'm going to say deep cleaning the oven because I really hate that job.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: I hardly ever do it.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: I don't like any of those, but we'll find out the answer at the end of the programme.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Now, the first project we're going to look at is on the remote Indonesian island of Rote.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Here, men traditionally work as rice farmers or fishermen, while women look after the home, the children and older people.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: But with few washing machines and no running water, these domestic chores take a long time.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: The NGO ARUNGI runs a project trying to change attitudes about the role of the island's women.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: They work alongside community leaders like Mama Shilpa, who spoke with BBC World Service reporter Ade Mardiyati.

transcript.speaker: Mama Shilpa
transcript.text: It is expected that the tasks done in the house, like holding the child, feeding the child, washing dishes, cooking, will all be done by the mother.

transcript.speaker: Ade Mardiyati
transcript.text: Shilpa tells me these are all considered women's work.

transcript.speaker: Ade Mardiyati
transcript.text: And you might be thinking, "Well, the man is busy in the fields, so it's just a fair division of labour."

transcript.speaker: Ade Mardiyati
transcript.text: But Shilpa tells me women also help out in the fields.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: On Rote, cleaning, cooking and sweeping are considered women's work – a negative term for boring and repetitive tasks which are traditionally done by women.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: Many cultures have a division of labour – a way of organising work where different tasks are done by different groups of people.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: But on Rote this means women work even harder, helping out with the farming and fishing too.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: You might think this only happens in traditional societies, but research suggests that women in wealthy countries also spend much more time on unpaid care work than men.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: One such country is Croatia, where the NGO Status M run their Superdads project.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Project worker Anamarija Sočo leads workshops encouraging dads and sons to take some of the pressure off mums.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Here, she explains the benefits of this to the BBC World Service.

transcript.speaker: Anamarija Sočo
transcript.text: Mothers have, you know, of course, more space for their careers, or hobbies, or just simply to rest – I mean, just to take a breather.

transcript.speaker: Anamarija Sočo
transcript.text: Women tend to especially appreciate men who do these kinds of chores.

transcript.speaker: Anamarija Sočo
transcript.text: And when they start pulling their weight, then they jokingly say that, "Uh yeah, women tend to nag less."

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: Sometimes mums need to take a breather – an informal way of saying stop and rest a while.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Anamarija also thinks women appreciate it when their husbands pull their weight.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: If you pull your weight, you work as hard as everyone else.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: Both these NGO projects agree about one thing – men doing more to help around the house results in happier homes, even if that means cleaning the toilet now and then.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: And speaking of cleaning the toilet, what was the answer to your quiz question, Neil?

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: I asked you what chore is the most hated in Britain.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: I thought it was cleaning the oven.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Well, I'm afraid that's not the right answer.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: People hate cleaning the windows even more than scrubbing the oven.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Apparently, 23% of the people who did the survey said cleaning the windows.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Let's recap the vocabulary we've learned, starting with chores – household tasks like cleaning, washing and ironing that have to be done regularly.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: If you do your fair share of work, you do a reasonable amount.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Women's work is a negative term for the boring and repetitive tasks which are stereotypically done by women.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: The division of labour is a way of organising work where different tasks are done by different groups of people.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: The idiom take a breather means to stop what you're doing for a short time and rest.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: And finally, if you pull your weight, you work as hard as everyone else doing the same job.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: Once again, our six minutes are up, but remember, you can find a free transcript including all the vocabulary on our website, at bbclearningenglish.com.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: Goodbye for now.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Goodbye!

listening.task: 출근길 운전하면서 한 번은 대략적인 내용만 듣고, 저녁에 두 번째는 스크립트를 보면서 들어요. 그다음 퀴즈에 답해 보세요. 'fair share', 'division of labour', 'take a breather', 'pull your weight'가 나오는 부분을 잘 들어 보세요.

quiz.q: According to the Good Housekeeping survey, what is the most hated household chore in Britain? a) deep cleaning the oven, b) scrubbing the toilet, c) cleaning the windows
quiz.answer: c) cleaning the windows. 응답자의 23%가 창문 닦기를 가장 싫어한다고 했어요. Pippa는 오븐 청소라고 했는데 틀렸어요!

sentences.text: Do you do your fair share of household chores?
I'm going to say deep cleaning the oven because I really hate that job.
sentences.ko: 오븐 대청소라고 할게요. 그 일이 정말 싫거든요.

sentences.text: Sometimes mums need to take a breather – an informal way of saying stop and rest a while.
sentences.ko: 엄마들도 가끔은 한숨 돌릴 시간이 필요해요.

sentences.text: If you pull your weight, you work as hard as everyone else.
sentences.ko: pull your weight는 다른 사람만큼 열심히 일한다는 뜻이에요.

sentences.text: People hate cleaning the windows even more than scrubbing the oven.
sentences.ko: 사람들은 오븐 닦기보다 창문 닦기를 더 싫어해요.

reading.title: Are some salts healthier than others?
reading.source: The Economist (public reprint via Hindustan Times)
reading.summaryKo: 핑크 히말라야 소금, 플뢰르 드 셀 같은 비싼 소금도 결국 대부분 염화나트륨이라, 미량 미네랄로 건강 효과를 보려면 하루 30g 이상(WHO 권장량의 6배) 먹어야 한대요. 의미 있는 첨가물은 두 가지뿐: 아이·임산부에게 중요한 요오드(iodine), 그리고 나트륨 일부를 대체하는 칼륨(potassium). 중국 농촌 약 2만 1천 명 연구에서 칼륨 강화 소금(나트륨 75% + 칼륨 25%)이 혈압을 낮추고 뇌졸중·심혈관 사건·사망 위험을 약 13% 줄였어요. 그래도 가장 간단한 방법은 소금을 덜 먹는 것이고, 신장질환이 있으면 칼륨 과다에 주의해야 한대요. 검사실에서 Na/K 수치를 보는 입장에서 읽으면 더 재미있을 거예요.
excerpt: HUMANS NEED salt. It contains sodium, which draws water out of cells to hydrate the bloodstream; enables muscles to contract and relax; and helps the intestines absorb nutrients. But one can have too much of a good thing.
Despite their differing appearances and price points, most supermarket salts—from fleur de sel to pink Himalayan—predominantly consist of plain old sodium chloride.
reading.tip: Economist는 말장난을 좋아해요: 'more than a grain of truth'(일리가 있다), 'taken with a pinch of salt'(곧이곧대로 믿지 않다), 'worth their salt'(제 몫을 하는) 모두 소금(salt/grain/pinch)과 관련된 관용구예요. 하나씩 찾아보세요!

writing.prompt: Write 3–5 sentences in English: How do you and your family share the housework?
writing.question: Which chore do you do most at home, and which one do you hate the most?
writing.hint: 이런 표현을 써 보세요: At home, I usually ... / My least favourite chore is ... / I try to do my fair share by ...

speaking.prompt: In one minute, talk about salt and your diet. Do you try to eat less salt? Is it easy with Korean food?
phrases: I try to eat less salt because ...
Korean food is often salty, for example ...
One easy way to cut down is ...
speaking.alt: 쉬운 버전: Say three short sentences about your meals (e.g. I like kimchi. It is salty. I eat less soup now.).
